lesson.title: A War to End All Wars: America Joins the Fight
lesson.summary: After nearly three years of official neutrality, escalating German submarine attacks and the shock of the Zimmermann Telegram led Woodrow Wilson to ask Congress for a declaration of war in April 1917, a war he framed as a fight to make the world safe for democracy.
lesson.body:
American neutrality in the European war had always been under strain. The sinking of the British passenger liner Lusitania by a German U-boat on May 7, 1915, killed 1,198 people, including 128 Americans, and provoked a wave of anger, though Wilson chose diplomacy over war at the time. Germany, wary of drawing America into the conflict, eventually pledged in 1916 to stop sinking passenger and merchant ships without warning, a commitment known as the Sussex pledge. That restraint did not last.

As explained in the previous chapter, German military leaders decided in early 1917 that unrestricted submarine warfare gave them the best chance to defeat Britain quickly, even at the risk of provoking the United States. Germany announced the resumption of this policy on January 31, 1917, and Wilson responded by breaking diplomatic relations with Germany on February 3, 1917. Weeks later, the Zimmermann Telegram was published, revealing Germany's proposal to help Mexico attack the United States, and German submarines soon sank several American merchant ships in the Atlantic. Wilson concluded that neutrality was no longer possible.

On April 2, 1917, Wilson addressed a joint session of Congress and asked for a declaration of war against Germany. He argued that the United States had no selfish ends to serve and framed American participation as a mission to make the world, in his words, safe for democracy. The Senate voted 82 to 6 in favor on April 4, and the House of Representatives followed with a vote of 373 to 50 on April 6, 1917, when Wilson signed the declaration into law. Opposition, while a clear minority, was not silent. Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana, the first woman ever elected to Congress, voted against the declaration, and pockets of antiwar sentiment persisted among Socialists, some labor activists, and German American communities.

Entering the war exposed a glaring problem: the United States had a peacetime army of only a few hundred thousand soldiers, nowhere near enough for the industrial-scale trench warfare underway on the Western Front. Turning a nation of civilians into an army capable of fighting in France would require mobilizing manpower on a scale the country had not attempted since the Civil War, the challenge taken up in the next chapter.
